speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
maintopic: MR. T. C. DOUGLAS EXPRESSIONS OF CONGRATULATION AND WELCOME TO LEADER OF NEW DEMOCRATIC PARTY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on behalf of the government I welcome back to this house an hon. member who has enjoyed one of the longest active political careers in Canada. Perhaps a few months have been missing here and there but, by and large, I believe he has been sitting in legislative chambers or parliaments since 1935.
We must all face the hazards of political life. The hon. member who has returned to this house has shown that he persists in the pursuit of his ideals, that he has great sticking power and that he believes strongly in the principles he follows. These are virtues we admire in him.
He is also welcome because he has a great sense of humour and conducts himself in a lively fashion in debates. Of course the hon. members of his caucus will welcome the additional leadership he will bring to their united ranks.

maintopic: MR. T. C. DOUGLAS EXPRESSIONS OF CONGRATULATION AND WELCOME TO LEADER OF NEW DEMOCRATIC PARTY
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: MR. T. C. DOUGLAS EXPRESSIONS OF CONGRATULATION AND WELCOME TO LEADER OF NEW DEMOCRATIC PARTY
speechtext:
We know he brings to the house an intimate knowledge of his new constituency, where he has been meeting his constituents for some months. He will find the
house a welcome place in which to be. It has changed a little. We now have a permanent or enduring Speaker, we have changed the rules a little, and some of the ministers are in the house, off and on.

maintopic: MR. T. C. DOUGLAS EXPRESSIONS OF CONGRATULATION AND WELCOME TO LEADER OF NEW DEMOCRATIC PARTY
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: MR. T. C. DOUGLAS EXPRESSIONS OF CONGRATULATION AND WELCOME TO LEADER OF NEW DEMOCRATIC PARTY
speechtext:
The one thing that has not changed, however, Mr. Speaker, is the courtesy of hon. members and the friendships which develop among members of all parties. As a human being and as a man devoted to principle, the hon. member stands second to none. Because of this we welcome him back to the house.

maintopic: MR. T. C. DOUGLAS EXPRESSIONS OF CONGRATULATION AND WELCOME TO LEADER OF NEW DEMOCRATIC PARTY

Mr. Speaker, we in this corner of the house congratulate the new member and leader of the New Democratic party on his election; we notice that though he has not been too fortunate in general elections, he seems to have become an expert in by-elections.
Mr. Speaker, we will now have the leader of the New Democratic party (Mr. Douglas) on our right, and even though we do not always endorse his ideas because they lean to the left, we nevertheless appreciate his many qualities as a parliamentarian. I have had the opportunity of knowing him personally in 1962. During all the debates, he was a credit to the House of Commons, by putting forward the ideas of his party which he represented very well.
I take the opportunity to commend those who, during his absence, assumed the leadership of the New Democratic party in parliamentary matters. Even though their leader was not here, they were able to hold out and set forth the ideas which prompted their constituents to elect them to the House of Commons.

speechtext:
I want, sir, through you to express my very sincere appreciation of the warm welcome which has been extended to me by members in all parts of the house, and particularly to say how deeply touched I am by the fine tributes which have been paid by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield), and the hon. member for Shefford (Mr. Rondeau), speaking on behalf of the Ralliement du Creditiste. I have been associated with politicians so long that I do not take too seriously what they say in their moments of euphoria; nevertheless I know from long experience and from having worked with members in all parties in this house that their tributes are sincere, and their welcome is a genuine one.
I am very happy to be able to resume my place in the house. As the Prime Minister has said, I have had many months away from the house in which to learn many things. I would even recommend it to some members of the house and of the government. I think that visiting logging camps, sawmills and pulp-mills, fishermen on their boats, businessmen and consumer groups is a very valuable experience for one who has been a long time in public life. I am deeply indebted to the house for its kindness, and to the people of Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands for the vote of confidence they gave to me and to my colleagues in sending me here.
I would like to express my appreciation to the members of the New Democratic party who sit in this house for the fine job they have done during my absence. I am glad the Prime Minister has noted the degree of unity which obtains. I have had no difficulty with some of them wanting to get out of NATO, and some wanting to stay in NATO.

maintopic: MR. T. C. DOUGLAS EXPRESSIONS OF CONGRATULATION AND WELCOME TO LEADER OF NEW DEMOCRATIC PARTY

They have managed to develop a degree of unity which I have found most comforting.
It was a great experience, coming back last night; when I got off the plane some of my colleagues and supporters met me and presented me with a book called, "The Sayings of Chairman Diefenbaker." When I got into our apartment I found sitting on the table, a book my wife had been reading, one by the Prime
February 20, 1969

Minister on federalism. In spite of those two very inauspicious beginnings I decided to take my seat, Mr. Speaker, and I would like to thank the members for their kindness and to say that at this very critical stage in Canada's history, when we are shaping the future of the country, I am very happy to be a member of the house. I hope that something of the experience which I have gathered may be of some value as we face the critical days ahead.

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald S. Macdonald (President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: STATEMENT AS TO LEGISLATION TO BE CONSIDERED BEFORE SUMMER ADJOURNMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a statement with regard to the business of the house for the balance of the session. I believe that the house may find useful some information that I have drawn together about the work remaining to be done between now and the beginning of the summer adjournment.
My proposal is that the house adjourn for Easter at the conclusion of the sitting on Wednesday, April 2 and sit again on Monday, April 14. I am proposing also that we should try to be ready to adjourn for the summer on Friday, June 27. On that basis, after yesterday, taking into account the two additional holidays prescribed by Standing Order 2, we now have 83 sitting days in which to complete our work.
Of those days a total of 18 are committed as allotted days for the business of supply with, I assume, an additional three days for the final supplementary estimates. I am reserving six days for a budget debate. Naturally, I cannot say whether the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) will want to initiate such a debate or, if he does, whether any budget bills will eventuate from his statement. This means that 27 days are committed. Any days that might be required for budget bills would be over and above that number. In other words, the maximum number of days that we can count on for the legislative business about which we now know is 56.
The House of Commons has before it, at some stage of the legislative process, a total
Business of the House
of 19 bills. In the other place there are four bills with which the House of Commons has not yet dealt. On the basis of the list put forward by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) on September 12, and my best knowledge at this moment, I can foresee 21 additional bills. This means that to the 19 bills now before this house at various stages we should add a total of 25 bills not yet before this house. There is also the matter of a proposed resolution dealing with Canada's anthems.
The following is a list of the bills not yet before the house and I should indicate that no significance should be attached, one way or another, to the order of this list: Investment companies Bill, S-17; Criminal Code (Hate propaganda) amendment, Bill S-21; Canada Shipping Act amendment, Bill S-23; Oil and Gas Productions and Conservation, Bill S-29; Canadian Educational Broadcasting Agency bill; Income Tax Act amendment-from the October 22, 1968 budget; Dominion Coal Board dissolution bill; Yukon Minerals bill; Canada Corporations Act amendment; National Housing Act amendment; Satellite Communications Corporation bill; Export Development Corporation bill; Federal Co-operatives bill; Old Age Security Act amendment; Loan Companies Act amendment; Trust Companies Act amendment; Canada Development Corporation bill; Indian Claims bill; Canadian and British Insurance Companies Act amendment; Foreign Insurance Companies Act amendment; Expropriation Act amendment; Statute Law (Superannuation) Amendment Act amendment; Fisheries Improvement Loans Act amendment (No. 2); Expo Winding-up bill; Patent Act (fees) amendment.
We also hope to introduce an industrial incentives bill in respect of the department of my colleague, the minister of regional and economic expansion, a Canada water bill and a securities bill, but it would not be our intention that these should be passed during the course of this session.
This schedule means that we are confronted with about 45 items to fill our remaining 56 days for legislation. I have made available to the house leaders of parties opposite a list showing the bills passed, the bills in progress in this house and the work to come.
Let me conclude by saying two things. First, it is always possible that emergencies will require the government to come to the house with additional legislative proposals not now anticipated. Secondly, if we finish our work before June 27 I will be more than

February 20, 1969

happy to join in a lobby for an earlier summer adjournment.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: STATEMENT AS TO LEGISLATION TO BE CONSIDERED BEFORE SUMMER ADJOURNMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have had the pleasure-perhaps I should correct that word of "opportunity"-of reading the list which has been placed before us by the President of the Privy Council. The government has the assurance of this party that, within the limits of our capacity and our right to discharge our responsibility as Her Majesty's Loyal Opposition, we will co-operate with the government in attempting to meet, as best we can, the schedule to deal with these legislative proposals within the time named. We do not however intend to be in any sense deficient in doing those things which as an opposition we have to do in the discharge of those responsibilities. I think I should make that quite plain, and I do so in no controversial spirit at all.
It is a fact that this has been an unusual session. There is the possibility of our having two budgets, at least time has been provided by the president of the Privy Council for this eventuality. There are a number of legislative proposals-and I am not going to be controversial about this either-which have been left over, but might well have been concluded in the normal course of events if the election had not been held. That was of course the right of the government.
If we can get all these things done by June 27, that is fine. If we have to stay a little longer, I and my colleagues will be very regretful, but we do not intend to be delinquent in the discharge of our responsibilities.
It is my hope that we can work out arrangements for business of the house. For today, for example, I am quite happy to propose that the legislation now before the house be completed today. This estate tax amendment legislation has had a great deal of consideration, and there has been an exceedingly good opportunity for debate. It has been canvassed from all sides of the house. I for one on behalf of this party would agree to an order, if the house is agreeable, to complete second reading, and go through the committee stage and third reading by staying today to complete this bill.
I would refer also to some of the other legislation before the house. For example I have in mind the Criminal Code amendment legislation. I understand from my colleagues who will be serving on the standing committee that when that measure goes to the standing committee it should not be impossible to work out an agreement, through consultation,

as to the length of time with which the committee should be seized of that bill. Once it has been before the standing committee, and the government is ready to report the bill, we will know what amendments there are.
In accordance with our views as expressed earlier in this house, once through the usual consultative processes among the house leaders we know what will be involved and what amendments will be brought back to the house we can decide without inhibition what period of time will be required at the report stage in the house.
Finally, before I sit down may I suggest that when we look at the bills we have been through, and look at the peripatetic progress that has been made, while I realize that members of the government must from time to time be away from this house-and I would not want to inhibit their right-under such circumstances it would facilitate the progress of legislation in the house, and other measures placed before us by the government, if when a measure was initiated and brought into the house for debate, the debate could be completed without having to suspend it, as has happened from time to time, and resume it at a later date. I think that more orderly and reasonable progress could be made if this were done. Having said that, Mr. Speaker, we are prepared to co-operate and we hope the target dates will be achieved. We wish the government success in at least reaching those target dates.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subtopic: STATEMENT AS TO LEGISLATION TO BE CONSIDERED BEFORE SUMMER ADJOURNMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, like the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin), I wish to thank the government house leader for having supplied us with a copy of the memorandum which he was using when he made his remarks. We believe it is very useful for us to know what legislation the government has in mind for the balance of the session. We also think it is useful and helpful to have a program so far as the calendar is concerned. I agree with the hon. member for Peace River that the important thing for this parliament to do is attend to its business even if we have to stay here, but we think it is a good idea to try and plan our time so we will get the important business done within reasonable time.
I should like to congratulate the government house leader upon including in the time schedule the necessary days for a budget presentation. He had to protect himself with respect to that matter, but we feel, because the
February 20, 1969
country deserves a statement as to our financial position and because it is important to the new program that we worked out as part of our procedures to have the budget in the spring, it would be a good idea to have the budget presentation at that time.
I am interested, of course, in noting that the government house leader has included the proposed Income Tax Act amendment so as to make an honest man out of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson), who is presently collecting a 2 per cent social disillusionment tax that has not yet been passed by parliament. In looking over the list of bills that we have before us, I am inclined to say that the important thing is not the number of pieces of legislation with which we are presented but the quality and value of those pieces of legislation. There are some notably missing. May I say a word or two about two or three which are on the list.
There is a reference to the Canada Development Corporation. This reminds me of the millions of times people pray "Thy kingdom come" but never expect it to happen. I hope that this time the government is going to go ahead with the Canada Development Corporation that has been mentioned so often. We trust that the housing legislation will have some real substance, some real content in it. I hope, too, that the reference to the Old Age Security Act and to the Statute Law (Superannuation) Amendment Act amendment means that we will not just be tidying up a few anomalies, but that the important needs which must be met under these acts will be dealt with at this session. I refer to the need for increased pensions.
I draw the minister's attention to the fact that there is not in the list any reference to the omnibus bill No. 2 to which the Minister of Justice (Mr. Turner) referred yesterday, nor is there any reference to any legislation arising out of the Woods report which is being considered by the Committee on Veterans Affairs. Consequently there is no reference to war veterans allowance under such legislation. We think this matter ought to be dealt with at this session. I have one other comment, Mr. Speaker. We welcome the reference to the Indian claims legislation that is to be dealt with at this session but, as has been stated on previous occasions, we feel that this legislation should not be proceeded with until the views of the native people of Canada have been heard with respect to it.
The government will have our co-operation in trying to get this program of legislation
Reference of votes to Standing Committees through within the target dates that have been suggested, but we urge, again, that what is important is the quality of the legislation. We plead for quality and substance in the legislation referring to the Canada Development Corporation, as well as in the legislation dealing with housing and matters related to pensions and to our war veterans.

subtopic: STATEMENT AS TO LEGISLATION TO BE CONSIDERED BEFORE SUMMER ADJOURNMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we, of the Ralliement Creditiste, can assure the government house leader of our entire co-operation regarding the legislative program we shall have to pass before the summer recess.
We have had the opportunity to become acquainted with the proposals already before us. Some bills require more careful consideration than others. That is why it is so difficult to come to a decision in advance as to the many pieces of legislation that the government intends to introduce and which have not as yet been tabled in this house, as we do not know yet their exact content.
At all events, according to the agenda submitted in conformity with the procedure, we shall have approximately 58 days, I think, to study the bills already before the house and those who are listed on the program we approved yesterday, and which was suggested in the house today.
Is it not strange that Saint-Jean-Baptiste Day which falls before June 27 is not mentioned before the adjournment of the house for the summer recess? Will we have to sit on June 24?
The government house leader did not mention this great feast day to which the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) attached so much importance last year, before the elections, and which was celebrated with great pomp in Montreal. I wonder whether we should attach a special importance to the celebration of Saint-Jean-Baptiste Day this year.

subtopic: PURCHASE PROGRAM TO STABILIZE FROZEN GROUNDFISH MARKET
PURCHASE PROGRAM TO STABILIZE FROZEN GROUNDFISH MARKET
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, our Canadian groundfish industry, as many hon. members know, is in difficulties. It is in difficulties because the export price for a number of our frozen groundfish products has declined sharply since 1967. This industry, which sells close to
DEBATES	5747
Stabilization of Frozen Groundfish Market 90 per cent of its output in the United States, is caught in a serious cost-price squeeze.
It is important to note that this squeeze has occurred despite the fact that the retail price for many of these products has continued to rise in the United States and elsewhere.
It is apparent, therefore, that the government's main objective must be to do what it can to bring about a permanent improvement in the marketing outlook for Canadian frozen groundfish products by reinforcing the industry's competitive position abroad. Such a program will be far more beneficial than shortterm subsidies. The latter can create serious difficulties because of Canada's international agreements on tariffs and trade. Also, experience has shown that subsidies cause few, if any, long-term improvements in incomes and working conditions in the industry.
The government therefore proposes, by taking advantage of our fisheries prices support legislation, to enter the market itself. It proposes, in other words, to initiate a purchase program designed to strengthen and stabilize market prices for frozen groundfish products. Supplies accumulated in this way will eventually be sold through ordinary commercial channels. They will not be released, however, at prices less than those paid for these stocks in the first instance. Nor will they be sold until their export price is high enough to cover our basic costs of production in Canada.
These costs must include an adequate price to our Canadian fishermen. The government is not prepared to enter into any plan to assist the industry unless appropriate measures are taken to ensure that the fishermen share in the benefits. Close to 15,000 fishermen and plant workers, and their families, depend upon the Canadian groundfishery, and their welfare must be of primary concern to the government.
It is our intention to maintain a close and continuing liaison with representatives of the fishermen and the trade in order to devise means whereby fishermen can be assured of prices that will not fall below the average for the years 1965, 1966 and 1967.
[DOT] (2:40 p.m.)
The low market prices of recent years have put many plants in the position where they lack working capital. Some have had to close for this reason. Others are in a precarious position at present and lack the necessary funds to modernize their operations and to cut costs by improving productivity.

Stabilization of Frozen Groundfish Market
In order to overcome this problem of a shortage of working capital, and in order to ensure adequate returns to fishermen, the government also proposes, as a special emergency measure, to make loans available to fishing and processing firms in 1969. The government is furthermore prepared to waive repayment of these loans until after the market price for our principal groundfish products reaches a figure which will ensure adequate returns to our Canadian fishermen and to the companies involved in our Canadian groundfishery.
Mid-term and long-term measures are also contemplated. Advice which the government has received from its consultants indicates that important economies can soon be achieved, both at sea and in our processing plants. Our Canadian groundfish industry will therefore be encouraged to avail itself of the financial assistance which is also available under our general adjustment assistance program. This program, as hon. members will recall, was instituted in order to help Canadian producers take advantage of growing export opportunities resulting from the Kennedy Round of tariff negotiations. Assistance under this program is available to firms which are prepared to restructure their operations in order to improve their competitive position between now and the early 1970s.
The results of this three-way approach must have an immediately beneficial effect on the frozen groundfish industry. The provision of loans under the conditions already outlined will help with the immediate problem of finding working capital. Use of the fisheries prices support legislation will strengthen the industry's hand in the market. And this, coupled with the greater efficiencies made possible through the adjustment assistance program will narrow the gap between production costs and market prices.
Looking even further ahead we must plan for greater rationalization in the industry. Certain plants will have to specialize in selected operations, and greater diversification in terms of products will be encouraged. It is apparent also that beginning in the early 1970s our frozen groundfish operations will have to be centralized in fewer growth centres. Such trends, though economically desirable, create related social and other problems. These must be resolved by taking advantage of companion programs being developed by our new federal departments of regional expansion and manpower. Also there
IMr. Davis.]

must be close liaison with the provinces
concerned.
The government, in co-operation with the industry, will continue to intensify its efforts to encourage greater use of our fishery products in both our domestic and export markets. Even a small increase in the per capita consumption of fish at home and in the United States can produce significant results. It is encouraging to note that consumption of frozen groundfish products has, in fact, been rising steadily on this continent. Also, as I said earlier, the ultimate consumer has been prepared to pay more for our fish.
There is therefore reason for optimism. This is especially true because fish stocks are definitely limited from the long term point of view. It follows that as production begins to level off, particularly in the North Atlantic, and as consumption continues to rise, prices should firm up as well.
This is why the government has decided to enter the market itself. Our objective is to firm up the price of Canadian produced fish to a level, or levels, more in line with long term trends. We believe, also, that through the operations of our fisheries prices support legislation we can help to stabilize the output of our Canadian groundfishery and achieve permanent improvements in the economics of an industry which shows every indication of being able to stand on its own feet in the long run.
This statement has dealt exclusively with the frozen groundfish industry. The government is also studying, very carefully, the problems of the salt cod industry, again from both a short and a long term point of view. As stated previously, there is now under way an examination of the possible advantages of a salt cod marketing board. I hope to be able to make an announcement regarding assistance for this important sector of our Canadian fishery in a few weeks time.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, hon. members on this side of the house listened with considerable interest to the statement made today by the Minister of Fisheries concerning the government's overall policy and program for the continued development of the fishing industry in Canada, with special reference to the development of the fisheries in the Atlantic provinces.
While we welcome the minister's belated announcement, I say to him in all seriousness that it is a statement which is long overdue. The groundfish industry in the Atlantic provinces has now experienced almost three years
February 20, 1969

of declining revenues and increasing costs. This condition has prevented any expansion in the earnings of fishermen and has resulted in operating losses for the processing industry which have been so heavy that a number of companies in the Atlantic provinces have been forced to close their doors.
I would point out that this period of difficult and disappointing financial experience followed one of expansion and modernization which began in 1958. From that year, up to 1966, investments in plants and fishing vessels was quite extensive and the optimism of our people was supported by strong demand and rising prices for the products of our industry.
The reversal of this expansionary trend is not due in my opinion to any weakening of consumer demand in our traditional markets or to any significant increase in raw material supplied to those markets. The causes of the serious financial dilemma faced by the freezing and the salt fish sectors of the Canadian groundfish industry are international tensions and the devaluation of foreign currencies, resulting in lower prices in our traditional markets. In the intense competition to sell frozen fishery products in the American market, our Canadian exporters were able to hold their own in terms of quality and quantity, but our position was retained only at tremendous financial cost. In fact, if the deficiency payment program had not been implemented from May to October in 1968, there is little doubt that still more of our fish processing companies would have found it necessary to close their doors.
This situation only serves to create further unrest and concern among thousands of our fishermen and their families who must depend upon processors to purchase their production, and their concern is sharpened by the knowledge that in hundreds of fishing communities there are no alternative occupational opportunities.
The government has proposed, by taking advantage of the fisheries prices support legislation, to initiate a purchase program designed to strengthen and stabilize market prices for frozen groundfish products. There is no indication in the minister's statement of the prices to be paid, or of the arrangements which will be made to hold these stocks. I would point out that fisheries products are not wheat. We are dealing here with a highly perishable commodity, one which must be kept in well controlled refrigerated conditions. I therefore suggest that to make this program effective it will be necessary to place
Stabilization of Frozen Groundfish Market greater emphasis upon the marketing of frozen fish. I hope the minister will enlist the good offices of the Secretary of State for External Affairs, who will be able to discuss this matter at the United Nations.
I hope, also, that he will enlist the aid of the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce, because if this part of the stated program is to be effective much greater emphasis will need to be placed on marketing. I wonder whether the minister has given any thought to discussing with representatives of the industry the possibility of co-operative marketing.
The minister also told us that the government proposes as a special emergency measure to make loans available to fishing and processing firms, and that it is prepared to waive repayment of these loans until after the market price for our principal groundfish products has reached a figure which will ensure adequate returns to our Canadian fishermen and to the companies involved in the groundfish sector of the industry. This particular statement is somewhat vague. I can only express the hope that the interest rates to be charged on these loans will not be so high that the means will destroy the end which the government hopes to achieve.
The minister also stated that beginning in the early 1970s frozen groundfish operations will have to be centralized in fewer growth centres. This, I hope, will not necessarily be the same growth centres used by the minister of resource development. It may well be that by using this measure to develop some of the outlying areas of the Atlantic provinces this could well be of assistance to the over-all development of the entire industry. It is obvious that in implementing any program the government's prime concern should be the price that is received by the Canadian fisherman. It should be adequate enough to enable him to provide for the needs of his family in today's inflated, high cost society.
[DOT] (2:50 p.m.)
Finally, I note that the government is preparing a study of the salt fish industry. Looking at it from the short and the long term point of view, I would recommend that the minister study the previous report made on this matter by a royal commission. I am sure he will find that very helpful. It is a very complex problem and I hope he can resolve it favourably on behalf of the fishermen and the processors. In any event, the minister has now weighed anchor and set a course. Like

Mr. Speaker,
I should like to emphasize that while the statement has been lengthy the fishing industry, especially on the Atlantic and the Pacific coasts, is so terribly important to the total Canadian economy that the necessity for such a lengthy statement outweighs the disadvantage of having to go through it in detail. The announcement of the minister, as I see it, envisages the prospect of the government's entering into the buying and marketing of fisheries products, with an extension of the machinery for making loans to the industry in order to help it over a difficult period.
One aspect indicates a relatively new venture and proves, I think, what we have been alleging for a long time, namely that about the only element of our society that can protect the economic and social position of people who find themselves harshly done by in this so-called free enterprise system is the government. The minister has finally realized that this is also the case in this situation.
Regretfully I fear that the attempt to try to see that the income of fishermen does not fall below the average for the years 1965, 1966 and 1967 will not be that helpful, because this particular industry has been in great difficulty for a very long time. It is simply an attempt to maintain the income of fishermen at its present poverty level. Some more dramatic moves are required in this regard in addition to those announced by the minister.
The minister stated that this step has been necessary because the industry and the fishermen in the industry found themselves caught in the cost price squeeze. One result of this has been the problems faced by the groundfish industry.
Not too many weeks ago a number of mergers, takeovers and closures on the west coast were announced in the fishing industry. The Weston Corporation virtually owns, controls and dominates the fishing industry on the west coast. The reason given for the closing of certain canneries and plants on the Pacific coast, for certain mergers of companies, purchase of their assets and so on, was that the industry there found itself in the cost price squeeze and could not operate economically any longer in the manner it had in the past.


In Prince Rupert alone, because certain canneries have closed down and will not be operating this year, and as a result of the mergers that have taken place, there is a good prospect that 1,500-that figure is arguable, but it has been used as a round figure- shore workers, people working in and around the canneries, will be unable to find employment in the fishing and the salmon industries this summer. There is a great necessity for the minister, this new department of regional and economic expansion and the department of Indian affairs, to do something immediately with respect to the situation on the west coast.
Whether the venture that is being entered into, as announced by the minister, is going to do something that is really worth while, as far as the fisherman is concerned, is rather doubtful because the (Objective has simply been to see that the income of the fisherman does not fall below the 1965, 1966, and 1967 average income for fishermen. As I say, as far as we are concerned it is merely maintaining their income at the poverty level; nothing is being done to bring the real fruits of a just society to these people. If the minister had accepted but one small part of the ideas that party has advocated for years, the fishing industry would be a lot better off than it is now.

speechtext: The house resumed, from Wednesday, February 19, consideration of the motion of Mr. Benson that Bill C-165, to amend the Income Tax Act and the Estate Tax Act, be read the second time and referred to a Committee of the Whole, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Saltsman (p. 5191).

subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND ESTATE TAX ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a few brief remarks in respect of this bill in order to pull together the ideas or criticisms put forward by my colleagues during this debate. I want to say to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) that my colleagues and I have given very careful attention to this bill and have come to the conclusion that it is not possible for us to support it for reasons which I will shortly indicate.
5760	COMMONS
Income Tax Act and Estate Tax Act
First, in order to make very clear the difference in our position from that of the Conservative party and its spokesmen who have taken part in this debate, may I say that we of the New Democratic Party are in favour of appropriate and equitable estate taxes. We regard a proper and equitable taxation system as being one that should serve three purposes. First, it should, of course, raise the revenue necessary to pay for the public services. Second, it should do this in such a way as to redistribute income and wealth. Third, it should be a system which would assist economic growth.
We believe, and I have always believed, that an estate tax is a necessary tax for the purpose of redistributing income and wealth in society. No one benefits more from the collective efforts of our total society than the son or daughter of a father who, no doubt through his own efforts, his capacity and hard work but also no doubt as a result of the organization of society as a whole and the organization of its economy, has been able to amass some savings, large or small, which he hands over to his children. When a child inherits wealth at an adequate level there is no reason in the world that that child should not pay taxes toward keeping the collective society going for all the people of this country in which he or she lives and works.
So we wish to make very clear and underline as strongly as I can that we favour an equitable and fair estate tax. When a person inherits considerable wealth that person ought to pay a fair share of that wealth in order to help carry on the business of the country and maintain all the other amenities from which he and his late father benefited in order to have the wealth which is now being distributed to the child.
We also make very clear that we are strongly in favour of the amendment to the estate tax contained in the bill which refers to elimination of the tax when the inheritance goes to the spouse. We recognize that it is useful when a spouse inherits from her husband, or indeed when a husband inherits from his wife, that there should not be a tax at that point and that the estate is more appropriately taxed when it passes to a stranger or the children. So we are in favour of an estate tax and very strongly support this amendment in so far as it removes the tax from the spouse who inherits the estate.
There are other aspects of the bill, however, which we cannot support. There are other aspects with regard to the reform of our taxation structure which must be taken into

DEBATES	February 20, 1969
account. We cannot support the minister's bill because contrary to what he and many members of his party have said during this debate the bill is not truly progressive and the rate structure is not equitable. That is the reason the hon. member for Waterloo (Mr. Saltsman) moved the amendment to the bill that it be not read the second time. We want an investigation of the entire estate tax structure to provide truly progressive and equitable rates in that structure.
The minister can talk for as long as he likes and hon. members behind him can speak for as long as they like but the fact remains that it is the low value estates in respect of wjhich we should be concerned, the estates involving amounts between $50,000 and $100,-
000.	These are the estates about which I am most concerned. I am much less concerned about the people who inherit from estates involving half a million dollars, $1 million or $2 million. They are not constituents of many members of the house; there are not very many of them. As a result of the progress made in the economy and more particularly as a result of collective bargaining there is a growing number of people in this country who, because they now have pension plans and life insurance policies which they did not previously have, are in the group of working people who may have estates valued at over $50,000.

speechtext: I appreciate that, Mr. Speaker, but I am not talking about wives at this point. I am talking about the point at which the estate, having been first given to the wife, is distributed on her death to the children.

subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND ESTATE TAX ACT

speechtext:
The pension may be gone but the estate is distributed to the children and may involve homes and whatnot. As a result of these developments-and whether or not the pension is entirely gone depends on whether the pension is taken in a lump sum- it may become part of the wife's estate. It may be taken in monthly payments, but if it is taken in a lump sum then by some kind of actuarially related lump sum it forms part of the wife's estate which may later be handed over.
What I am saying, without arguing with the minister about the details-and I am
February 20. 1969

happy to say, this-is that there will be greater numbers of people in Canada in the future than has been the case in the past leaving relatively small estates of $60,000, $65,000 or $70,000. The total number of people who will likely leave estates-I think the minister used this figure and I am told by other advisers perhaps not as competent as he but competent-which will be taxable is only about 5 per cent. So we are still talking about a very small number of people. Of that proportion there will be an increasing number of lower value estates included.
No matter how much the minister may argue about it, the fact is that his own tables, copies of which he supplied us, show that in the $50,000 to $150,000 level of estates, as a result of his amendment, the rate is higher and the amount paid is higher. In the case of a $60,000 estate, and I am doing this from memory but I am sure I remember correctly, the amount paid becomes $4,800 instead of $2,600 when the estate is eventually handed over.
The minister and hon. members sitting behind him continue to refer to the case where the estate is first deeded to the wife and when she dies goes to one child. If he looks at his tables he will find that in the case of a $60,000 estate it does not relate only to one child. If it involves one child the amount is $4,800 compared with $2,600. If there are two children the amount is $3,000 as against $2,600. The rate is increasing.
The other case to which the minister and the members behind him constantly point is the case where a stranger is involved in part of the bequest. Certainly the case here involves an estate left outright to a widow or stranger and an estate divided equally among the adult children. I am not going to argue with the minister across the floor because I would be out of order in any case, but I am satisfied after a careful study of these figures, as my colleagues are satisfied, that the tax which the minister is proposing is regressive at the bottom end of the scale. In some of the more important cases where the estate would be handed over the rate would be higher at the bottom end and the tax again would be higher. Let us relate that to what the economists call the effective rate rather than the marginal rate.
I hope you will forgive me for explaining that the marginal rate is the lowest rate applicable to the particular size of estate with which we are concerned. The effective rate is the rate of tax which in fact is being imposed on the taxable part of the
Income Tax Act and Estate Tax Act estate after you have taken off the $50,000, let us say, and whatever other exemptions you may have the right to deduct. If you look at the effect of this tax structure the minister has presented to the house in terms of the effective rate, in other words, the rate which is applied to the taxable part of the estate, you will discover a really scandalous result.
If the taxable part of the estate is $1,000, $5,000 or $10,000, the effective rate is 50 per cent of those taxable amounts. If you get to the point where the taxable part of the estate is $30,000, the effective rate is 36 per cent. When you get to $50,000 the rate is 31.2 per cent. When you have a taxable part which is $100,000 the rate is only 29.7 per cent. If it is $150,000 the rate is only 23.4 per cent. After that it begins to climb again. So this is a regressive structure in terms of the rate that applies to the taxable part of the estate which, after all, is the part of the estate that is relevant in these discussions.

In some cases estates of $1 million or $1,500,000 will carry less tax as a result of this amendment than was the case under the old law.
I think the minister got himself into this position, and I give him the benefit of the doubt by thinking he was trying to make a genuine reform in this area of our tax structure, by making an a priori decision, the reason for which I cannot understand unless it was the result of pure conservatism with a small "c", if the Leader of the Opposition will permit me to use that word in respect of the Minister of Finance. He made an a priori decision that he would not raise any more from this tax under his new rates than he raised before. I think he said he would raise $2 billion altogether but would not raise any more through this tax. So when he came to the top, in order to achieve that totally undesirable purpose, he reduced the rate from 54 per cent to 50 per cent and then had to increase the rate at the bottom in order to make up the differences that might arise. The minister has had the Carter report for a long time. When you have an estate tax structure such as the minister now proposes, you do not take into account the income of the legatee. If one member of a family has been successful in his profession and already has half a million dollars and another member of the family has been unsuccessful in his work in a factory, and each gets $100,000 from the estate, under this proposal they each pay the same tax. The minister gets himself into that box because he is saying he is reforming our tax structure. But he is doing it piecemeal. He is dealing with the estate tax now, and I understand from something I read the other day that he will probably deal with income tax next. I do not know whether this means that at that time he will not deal with any other tax such as a capital gains tax or any of the other taxes that may be involved.
We in this party are convinced, and I would be very surprised if most members of the house did not agree, that one of the bases of any decent and just society is a just taxation structure. There is nothing more signifi-

cant about the criterion of equity in a society than the tax structure which the people have to bear. If the tax structure is unfair and inequitable, if it falls on the lower incomes unfairly, if it hits the working people and the low income farmers unfairly, if it is a tax on property which is regressive, then you have one of the major unjust components in a society. If the tax structure is genuinely progressive, if you take it off the back of the home owner, if you make the tax on the lower income people equitable so that anyone with a family who is making about $4,000, which is what we have suggested, should pay no tax at all, so that there is a minimum amount on which the family may live, if the tax structure is built from there on up in order to genuinely redistribute income and wealth, then you have one of the important elements of a decent and just society. That is what we ask for.
I have a philosophy which tells me that no one person in our present society makes economic gains or economic progress on his own. I reject the notion which I have heard repeated time and time again by hon. members of the Conservative party in this house, that this fellow worked hard. Sure he did. And for every fellow who works hard and makes a million dollars there are five million fellows who work hard and cannot make a million cents. So it is not merely the hard work that produces wealth; there are other things that produce it-the total environment of society and all the tools that society gives a person with which to make wealth.
If I am a successful lawyer-assume that I am for the moment-it was not done by my own efforts. I used a law school that was built for me. I used the law libraries that were built for me, and the whole wisdom and experience of generations that somebody attempted to put into my dull head. It is the collection of all this experience over the ages, the school which was collectively provided for me and the libraries which I used which were collectively provided for me, and all that goes with them that taught me my profession. I am talking nonsense if I stand up and say I make X thousands of dollars a year by my own efforts. The deuce I do. I do it as a result of the total social environment of which I am a product, which gave me the opportunity to get the kind of education and training that enables me to command a higher income. That is no reason why I should hang on to it. On the contrary, it is a very good reason why I should pay a large part of it to the state, to society, to make up for those

millions of others who mainly for economic and social reasons were unable to get the same education and the same training so that they might make a higher economic income and have a higher standard of living.
It is in that context, as well as in many others, that we are determined to demand a proper reform of our taxation system, the application of the basic principles of Carter, the application of those principles which will make the tax structure a component, as I have said, of a just and decent society instead, as it is now in many instances, of a burden on those least able to bear it.
The Minister of Finance and the government cannot do that kind of job and will not do that kind of job because (a) they apparently do not believe in it, (b) they do not intend to, and (c) the minister is going about it in a piecemeal way. That is not the way to reform the tax structure. The greatness of the Carter report, whether or not one agrees with every word in it, is that it looked at the tax structure as a whole. It related each part. It related the question of what it called vertical equity to horizontal equity and all the other matters that go into a proper tax structure. The minister has not done that.
Certainly there are some improvements in the amendments before the house. There are many instances where one has to support a bill, even though one is not satisfied with it, because it makes some improvement. But that is not the case here. The improvements are not good enough, and as part of a total revision of our tax system the bill is a miniscule crumb. I did not say the minister was crummy. I leave it to other members of this house to describe people that way. I just said the bill was a miniscule crumb. We in this party do not intend to vote for so small and so ineffective an amendment. Indeed, we will fight, not only in this case but later when other reforms to our tax structure are put forward, for a genuine tax revision, for a really equitable tax structure. We do not intend to accept amendments such as these which do not accomplish anything in the way of fundamental justice for the people of Canada, except for the spouse, and that is not good enough for us to support the bill as a whole.

I want to congratulate the Minister of Finance. It was suggested yesterday by one hon. member that we who support the government are under instructions to vote as the government directs. Let me tell the house that I have never received any such instruction.
I say to hon. members that if changes had not been made in the earlier proposals I would have been glad to stand up for my constituents and vote against the government on this measure. Changes have been made, however. They are changes which should probably have been introduced years ago, but the fact is that they were not introduced and now they have been. The situation for years, under both Liberal and Conservative governments, was that if a man died leaving money which both he and his wife had accumulated in partnership, the wife had to pay estate duty. This was the position not only in Canada but in many other countries. Now, for the first time, the Minister of Finance has recognized the fact that a husband and wife are a team who accumulate their estates together. In future, no matter how much the one leaves the other will have to pay no succession duty whatsoever. I congratulate the Minister of Finance on making this possible, and members of the opposition should congratulate him too.

Mr. Speaker, it is often said these days that there are no real differences between the political parties in the country. We are told that ideology is dead. I think that the legislation before this house and the attitude taken toward it by the different parties proves exactly the contrary. It reveals a wide difference of political philosophy on the part of members of this house.
The Conservatives, if I judge correctly from their remarks, basically seem to be against an inheritance or estate tax. On the
February 20, 1969

Income Tax Act and Estate Tax Act other hand, the Liberals, in the name oi reform, bring in some minor improvements to a regressive and inadequate tax system and reject any basic change in the system. The New Democratic Party stands for a new taxation system which would be demonstrably fairer, that would secure the additional revenue urgently needed if there were a reduction to be made in the crushing burden of taxation on people in the lower income groups.
We are opposed to this legislation not because we are opposed to an estate tax; quite the contrary. We believe that an inheritance or estate tax is one of the fairest means available to raise revenue. Generally speaking, an inheritance tax falls on those best able to pay, especially if we make sure, as we should, that widows and dependants are totally exempt and that the family is treated, as it ought to be, as a unit. It is also true that an inheritance tax with these exemptions falls due precisely at the time it can most easily be paid without hardship to anyone.
We in this party are opposed to the tax proposed in the bill because it deliberately repudiates the basic philosophy of using the tax system as an instrument of social justice, as an instrument to promote equality between Canadians. We oppose this legislation because it jettisons some of the main proposals contained in the Carter commission report for a fairer, more equitable system of taxation.
There has been a lot of talk about the Carter system. What, in effect, was the system recommended by the Royal Commission on Taxation? It will be remembered that it was a six-volume report of some 2566 pages. It was the product of four and a half years study by more than 150 tax experts. Some people may sneer at the accountants, tax lawyers, economists and others who prepared the report. I do not. I respect them for producing detailed proposals to create a completely new system of taxation in Canada based on equity and fairness. They were not doctrinaire socialists. Nor, as a matter of fact, do I consider myself to be a doctrinaire socialist. They took a careful look to see what was required to give Canada a tax system that would remove the undue burden of the existing tax system from the poor and place a greater burden upon those who can afford to pay, a burden on those who can afford to pay, without exemptions or chiselling.

The basic proposal of the commission was that all forms of income, regardless of source, should be treated alike for tax purposes, whether that income comes to the recipient in the form of gifts or inheritances, in the form of capital gains, in the form of earned income or income earned on property. Whatever was received would then be taxed on a progressive basis with generous exemptions at the lower level and a rising scale at the higher level.
I suggest that this is simple justice. Indeed, it is recognized in our present income tax structure. But very limited effect is given to this principle. In cases where income is earned from such sources as capital gains, gifts or inheritances, or from profits from certain tax-exempted income, there is either no tax at all-a complete exemption from tax- or there is a regressive rather than progressive taxation. Applying this general principle to the field of estate and inheritance taxes and taxes on gifts, the report of the royal commission on taxation recommended that the existing estate and gift tax acts be repealed. It also recommended that henceforth all gifts ought to be brought under the recipient's comprehensive income tax base and taxed at full, progressive rates in the same way as salaries, wages, business income, dividends, interest, capital gains, and windfalls ought to be taxed. To that proposal I say: Why not implement it? To use a crude but current expression, a buck is a buck, no matter what its source. The Minister of Finance says no. In my view the Royal Commission on Taxation was perfectly correct in saying that a buck is a buck, and the minister is wrong. A buck is a buck and ought to be treated as such.
Let me say this, Mr. Speaker. My party supports the contention that no gifts or inheritances between members of a family unit, between husband, wife and dependent children, ought to be taxable. The commission proposed that existing, gaping holes in the tax network ought to be patched so as to Capture certain large gifts made by wealthy people. The result of adopting these proposals would have been a substantial increase in government revenue. The commission estimated that revenue from these sources of $140 million annually would be increased to $350 million if certain of its proposals were adopted.
February 20, 1969
I ask this question, Mr. Speaker. Does the minister despise raising money from wealthy people? Does he not wish to create the means or powers that will permit him to relax the burden of taxation crushing the small wage earner or home owner? He would have acquired these powers if he had adopted the commission's proposals. What does the minister say to the royal commission's proposals? What does he say ought to be done to put taxes in this country on an equitable basis? Although I have read the minister's speeches, I have not seen in those speeches any explanation of this point.
In the debate of February 5 the minister said that once the government had decided to retain the estate tax it was necessary for it to decide whether that tax, under its proposals, was being levied in the fairest possible way. The government considered but rejected the recommendations of the Carter Royal Commission on Taxation and rejected the suggestions regarding inheritance taxes. During that debate the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby (Mr. Broadbent) interjected and asked why the government was adopting that position and the minister replied in words to this effect: Because we have decided a buck is not a buck and because we have decided to keep the revenue yield about the same while instituting reforms to help widows, widowers and young children.
These reforms, Mr. Speaker, may have already helped some widows, widowers and young children of ample resources. The minister has already provided for generous exemptions on estates. Yet these reforms mean absolutely nothing for those earning less than $5,000 a year. If the recommendations of the commission had been implemented all taxes paid by those earning between $5,000 and $7,000 a year could have been reduced by 7 per cent. Those earning under $5,000 a year would have had their taxes reduced by 10 per cent. Farmers with incomes in the lower brackets would have benefited from these reforms. Speaking purely of income tax, it is estimated that if the commission's report were implemented those in the lower income brackets could save up to 40 per cent of their tax bills. Farmers in low income brackets would benefit particularly from such reforms.
Is it wrong to sympathize with those in the lower income brackets who must pay income
Income Tax Act and Estate Tax Act tax on a modest income and not to sympathize so much with those who are more prosperous and accumulate enough to pay estate taxes on death? I wish to make it clear that I consider special circumstances require special administrative remedies. I do not suggest for a moment that measures ought to be adopted which would, in some instances, cause the forced sale of farms to be undertaken. Implementing the recommendations of the royal commission would mean that farmers at the lower end of the income scale would pay lower income taxes.
In rejecting the recommendations of the commission the government is helping the rich. Because of pressures from special interests it seems that the government is not able to reduce taxes for those in the lower income scales who already are heavily burdened. The government has chosen to act in favour of the rich, who need its help least of all. We therefore feel obliged to reject this measure although it contains a modicum of reform. Indeed, the proposals before us seem to me to be unprincipled in the sense no principle is discernible behind them. They are regressive in their general application.
In voting in this house we all bear in mind the interests of those who elected us. The interests of most of my constituents, no doubt, are opposed to this bill-and here I am not thinking of the handful within the constituency of Greenwood who will accumulate or inherit estates large enough to attract inheritance taxes. Most of my constituents are working people earning between $4,000 and $7,000 a year. When one considers today's cost of living and the burden of taxation such people have to sustain, it is clear they cannot accumulate estates on which succession duty must be paid. But that does not mean they are not vitally concerned about the matter we are dealing with here. They are being crushed by the present taxation system which has been described, and rightly so, as illogical, inequitable and inadequate. If the government ignores the proposals of the royal commission it will have to raise most of its revenue from sources other than the rich. It will have to continue the time-honoured system, illogical, inadequate and unfair as it is, of soaking the small and moderate income earner and not soaking those who are best able to pay. I cannot vote for a measure containing such a glaring and explicit message, that the government rejects a fairer and more just taxation system.

He was unable to convince them they were on the way to disaster unless changes were made. This system was evaluated and there was no change by anyone with a sense of responsibility.
I quote from the statement made by the hon. member for York East:
The new rules are now in effect, in the House of Commons, and since you will recall that I fought for these changes for six years-
I can just see him. Were these changes as a result of the hon. member's ideas? I was

I am pleased to report that the business of the House of Commons will at long last progress with some efficiency. There have been some disappointments-
One can imagine his thoughts when he used those words.
-mostly in the composition and power of the committees, because although the committees have been given a great deal of work to do. the government members of the committee have been instructed to make no changes to the bills, coming before the committee, and to vote exactly as they are told by the government.

That is what you call letting the cat out of the bag. He revealed the facts. This member valiantly stood for six long years and fought to bring about a new efficiency in parliament, but when the changes were put through this arbitrary government said to Liberal members: "This is the way you will vote." The government could have saved a lot of time if it had provided a ballot for its supporters to fill in. That would have saved a lot of discussion in the standing committees.
If the bill before us were sent to a standing committee people from all over Canada would appear to criticize it, people from all walks of life, even those represented by the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Bas-ford). I was out in his area and everybody I met there asked: "Where are we going in this country with a government that spends and spends and spends, and taxes and taxes and taxes?"

At least time is set aside for one. The only hope the Canadian people have is that there will not be another budget because if there is the Minister of Finance will take another crack at them with taxes. The Minister of Finance has established for himself one of the most unenviable records for prophesy of any minister of finance in Canadian history. He prophesied that there would be a balanced budget. He was out by hundreds of millions of dollars. He prophesied that there would be only one budget. We got two within a year or a year and a half, and we are going to get another.
DEBATES	5769
Income Tax Act and Estate Tax Act
All across Canada people are asking, "When are we going to put an end to this spendthrift government?" I remember that when I was prime minister we spent $6 billion annually and it was said that was something terrible. Now the estimated expenditure is $13 billion. It rises all the time. But the ministers claim that they are a saving government. They save on those things where the savings are of no importance. When the Prime Minister decided that we were not going to fire guns off any more to honour the members of the royal family, all gave their acclaim. They said, "Isn't this wonderful? We are going to save $40,000. After all, there are better ways in which Canadians can show loyalty and devotion."
But then they added to the salaries of the highest paid civil servants tens and tens of thousands of dollars, and also added 50 per cent to the salary of the Governor of the Bank of Canada. "Be restrained, don't overspend, but let us go on and on," is their theory. That is what they are doing. But it is a surprising thing that while they do all these things they forget about the retired civil servants. Apparently they are not entitled to consideration. They forget about the veterans. They postpone and procrastinate but other expenditures mount and mount.
I shall be brief so that a vote can be taken at the earliest possible moment. I have tried through the years to follow a reasonably consistent course. I see an editorial in the Globe and Mail that has been subjected to some misinterpretation. It is entitled, "First-A Few Questions," and reads in part:
The members of the legislature think they need a raise in pay. Conservative Party Whip Leonard Reilly said last week that it was an all-party desire (naturally: this is the one area which only a John Diefenbaker would fail to recognize as non-partisan).
Some people have misinterpreted that. My attitude was clear and definite in 1963 when we raised our indemnities that the raise should not come into effect until an election enabled the Canadian people to approve. Some others had the same view, but I followed my vocal support of the principle that there should be no increases except after an election by actually doing something to which I have not referred previously. I repaid or made a grant to the government of Canada of the excess. In the year 1963 the gift amounted to $5,589.22, and in 1964 to $8,000. I returned those amounts to the Crown believing in a principle which apparently does not receive the support of the Globe and Mail if that
February 20, 1969

Income Tax Act and Estate Tax Act editorial is to be interpreted as apparently it was intended.
Surely we in parliament must give an example to the Canadian people. I have followed this course. It was not to my own benefit. But when I speak here I speak according to my conscience. The present government is increasing salaries in the high echelons while unemployment is mounting at a very high rate, at an inexcuseable rate because in the United States the trend is all the other way.
We had unemployment when I was in office, but the United States rate of unemployment was higher than ours. Today we have unemployment mounting when there is a general level of economic advance. People are beginning to ask, "Isn't it about time for Canadians as a whole to join in a tax revolution?" They do not mean a revolution in the ordinary sense of the term but rather to say to the government: "You have gone as far as you are going. You have increased our income tax twice. You hit us with this 2 per cent social development tax, which is a complete misnomer."
According to the premiers of the various provinces who spoke at the conference last week, the 2 per cent tax is the equivalent of seven or eight points in income tax. Where is all this going to stop? The government gives no indication that it will stop. The Minister of Finance showed a lot of courage and determination in refusing to permit amendments to his proposals until he was inundated with protests and forced to back up. Then he produced the monstrosity which we have before us today and which is designed to deceive the Canadian people. They tell us now, "You are going to have a $50,000 exemption." That is the story that is spread across the country by Liberal members-

-and the Minister of Finance has done nothing to half that unjust suggestion of a $50,000 exemption. If you have an estate of $49,999 you pay nothing. If you have an estate of $50,001 you pay on $30,001, as I understand it. In other words, they are taking the people of Canada for another ride while pretending that they have done something to help them.
Mention was made by a previous speaker that this is a tax on the poor, and that is what it is. Those in the lower income brackets who save during their lifetime are going to be pillaged in death. That is what it amounts to, and I for one will not support this bill in

any particular. I summarize its provisions as follows: the gift tax is greatly increased, from a present maximum of 28 per cent and accelerating to 75 per cent. Canadians do not realize yet what a ride they will get when this comes into effect because the government expects that those who might raise objection will be dead. They will be dead before there is a realization on the part of their legatees concerning the degree of taxation to which they will be subjected.
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
This bill in no way alters the views I expressed in April, May and June last when my friends of the N.D.P. in speeches all over the province of Saskatchewan said that this is great legislation, that it is lovely. I have the speeches here. I do not want to spoil Hansard by reading them. I shall epitomize them in this way: It is the finest thing ever; it will hit the rich. Let us see how it will hit the rich.

It was the estate tax that they were supporting. The hon. member is now trying to twist things. That is the reason for the N.D.P. amendment. It is for the purpose of getting themselves out of the cul de sac in which they find themselves as a result of subsequent events. They say, "tax the rich". This bill will strike a serious and widespread blow at Canadians everywhere. As I said a moment ago many people have been lulled into a false sense of security in the belief that it is confined to those with very large estates. As a matter of fact, on an estate of $6 million the amount paid will be less now than it was before. But who will pay the piper? It will be the smaller estates represented by the 5,700 Canadian estates taxed in the last year of record available. Eighty-two per cent of these estates are in the range of $50,000 to $300,000. These are the estates that will get hooked. When an estate reaches the figure $50,001 it is taxed on everything over $20,000.

To show how the little man will take the ride as I have stated 82 per cent of estates are between $50,000 and $300,000. Indeed, 70 per cent of that succession duty taxation has been levied on estates valued at less than $100,000. What does that mean? It means that a person who has saved or a farmer whose prices have been inflated will be subject to heavy taxation. The minister thought he had reduced something. First he said he would not change it and then he backed down and said, "Now you see it; it is fine; nobody is going to pay on anything up to $50,000". That is right. But when it reaches $50,001 that is when they catch them. This legislation will mean a drastic increase in taxes in respect of those who have saved during their lifetime to provide better opportunities for their families. This government has taxed and taxed.
The minister says there is no longer any danger that family and other small businesses will be ended. He says they are not going to allow these businesses to be sold. He says he will give them five years in which to pay. In other words, they will have five years of freedom from disaster; that is all. They are going to extend the extinction period by five years with regard to small businesses.
This legislation will spell the end of the family farm. A farmer's estate consists mainly of land and on that basis it will be almost impossible for most sons and daughters to inherit their father's farm. This is ridiculous. Here we have one minister spending money to keep young men and women on the farms and another minister taxing them off the farm. This legislation will seriously reduce the amount of funds available for investment and will unfavourably affect the development of Canadian industry by Canadians. If this bill becomes law it will diminish incentive, impoverish the provident who have worked a lifet'me to give their children better opportunities in life than they have had, and will ultimately virtually socialize the Canadian economy.
Apparently this is one of the phases of the government's plan for a just society. All I can say is th-t it is just for the benefit of the government that it is extorting and extracting further taxation from the people. It is the act of a money-grabbing government which has been on a spending spree. I should like to hear the minister say that he will put an end to this. Some of the ministers have suggested that the government should be careful not to go on spending and spending. The government did away with the firing of $40,000 worth of gunpowder. This was done really for
anti-monarchical reasons under the guise of being a saving of expenditure. I wish the minister would tell his co-spenders that this is the end and there is going to be no more increased taxation. I should like him to carry out his promise and that of his predecessors about a balanced budget, which we have not seen.
